item.title: Trump touts 3-hour meeting on ending the war after threatening to 'annihilate' Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Gram Slattery and Humeyra Pamuk UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump used his UN General Assembly speech on Tuesday to make the case for his war on Iran, arguing he has prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and warning that he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" if no deal is reached to end the conflict. While predicting his administration would strike a peace ‌deal with Iran following the November 3 US midterm elections, Trump called on other nations to join America in isolating Iran economically to force it to the negotiating table. "I have a big decision to ‌make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" Trump said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" He ​later told reporters at the United Nations that US officials had held a "very good" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on Tuesday. He subsequently appeared to clarify that special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had met with mediators rather than Iranian officials directly. "Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran, merely mediators," he told reporters at the start of a meeting with Gulf leaders at the UN. "Let's see what happens with that." Since returning to office last year for a second term, Trump has sent waves through the global order, joining Israel to attack Iran, ordering a raid on Venezuela that captured the country's leader, and threatening to seize Greenland. In a 37-minute speech ahead of a whirlwind diplomatic schedule that ‌included meetings with the leaders of Britain, Ukraine and Japan, Trump laid out ⁠his foreign policy vision, arguing that the Iran war had spared the world the threat of a nuclear-armed menace while asserting US dominance in the Western Hemisphere is essential to preventing crises from taking root. "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," Trump ⁠said. "While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace." Outside the UN headquarters, dozens of anti-Iranian-government demonstrators gathered, a few of them holding up signs calling for democracy and decrying dictatorship. Trump brushed aside suggestions that the midterm elections, in which his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress, could constrain his handling of the war. Some analysts have argued that a Democratic takeover of the legislature would weaken his leverage in the conflict. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running," Trump said, referring to the leadership ​in ​Tehran. "I did that already, and won in a landslide. We won in a giant landslide, and I'll be here for 2-1/2 years." DIPLOMATIC ​WHIRLWIND Taking aim at US neighbors, Trump labeled Mexico "the epicenter of cartel violence," urged its government ‌to "reclaim control of its soil," and said his administration was pursuing "a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba." Members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump referenced his pressure campaign against the country. "It's an absolutely failed state, it's failing like never before, and it will fall," said Trump. Yet Trump's appearance was less dramatic than in 2025, when he used a combative speech to chastise world leaders, warning that some countries were "going to hell," and complained about UN facilities after being briefly stranded on a malfunctioning escalator and suffering an initial teleprompter failure. Trump renewed his criticism of the UN, highlighting his efforts to cut its bureaucracy, but offered no fresh attacks or indications that the US would leave any additional UN agencies. Trump spoke less than a week after a UN fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe US forces committed war crimes in two strikes on Iran, including one that hit a primary school ‌in the southern city of Minab. He renewed his criticism of international bodies that could serve as a check on US power, singling ​out the International Criminal Court and declaring that US military personnel would not be subject to its authority. "We will never allow US service ​members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction ​over us," he said. Ahead of a UN Security Council meeting on AI and international security on Wednesday, Trump acknowledged the challenges of the new technology but said, "I'm not going to stifle ‌growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution." The speech kicked off ​a day of high-level diplomacy at the United Nations, where Trump ​was due to meet more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine continued to test his foreign policy agenda. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump in their first-ever meeting, where they discussed trade, Ukraine and the status of the Falkland Islands. Trump called Burnham a "natural business person" after the meeting. At the press-facing start of their talks, Japanese Prime Minister ​Sanae Takaichi said the meeting would demonstrate the strength of the US-Japan alliance amid ‌a "severe security environment, including in Asia," an apparent nod to China. Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later this week. Trump lavished praise on Takaichi, calling her a friend and ​predicting she would "go down as one of the great prime ministers." On his meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, Trump told reporters that the two talked about finding a solution to end Russia's ​war in Ukraine. item.title: Hegseth announces new Pentagon battlefield test for promotions to general
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Pentagon is altering the promotion process to get to the rank of general in an effort to “cut bureaucracy and demand true meritocracy” across the senior ranks, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Tuesday. In a video posted to social media , Hegseth declared the Defense Department this year will roll out the Joint Warfighter Evaluation, a new battlefield-style assessment for eligible colonels and Navy captains. The evaluation is intended to screen the officers aimed for one-star general or admiral on “their ability to fight, adapt, and win,” according to Hegseth. “While the backbone of our military is our NCOs [noncommissioned officers] and our petty officers, victory depends on the commanders who lead them,” Hegseth said in the video. “America needs warfighters who can master a chaotic battle space,” he added, later noting that commanders should be chosen by “proven competence, not paper credential.” He likened the new evaluation to the Louisiana Maneuvers — a mass series of military exercises done directly before the U.S. entered World War II, during which roughly 400,000 troops conducted a wargame to evaluate America’s training, logistics and commanders. Hegseth said such testing brought out leaders like former President Eisenhower, a five-star Army general who planned and carried out the Allied assault on the coast of Normandy and the liberation of Western Europe; Army Gen. Omar Bradley, the first chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who eventually oversaw the U.S. military's policymaking in the Korean War; and Adm. Chester Nimitz, who commanded Allied air, land and sea in the Pacific theater during World War II. The Joint Warfighter Evaluation “brings that standard to the modern multi-domain fight,” Hegseth said. “This evaluation is an objective equalizer. The scenario only cares about operational decisions under pressure.” Hegseth said he had tasked Stuart Scheller, the deputy chief of staff to the undersecretary of Defense for personnel and readiness, to lead the effort a year ago. Each military branch will have its own version of the evaluation, according to internal documents obtained by The Hill. The Army will use a written assessment then a digital wargame; the Air Force and Space Force will require a two-hour online analysis test followed by a one-hour interactive simulation; the Navy will have officers travel to the Naval War College for a three-hour written assessment then a two-to-three-hour wargame; and the Marine Corps requires an eight-hour remote evaluation on an AI-enabled platform combining written assessments and situational judgment tests, according to an internal memo. The Joint Staff will evaluate 50 to 60 Joint Forces Staff College students using a “hybrid” model with an independent written analysis followed by an “in-person, AI enabled execution phase” at Norfolk, Va. school, the memo said. The current system has promotion boards that consider officers via their accumulated evaluations from their superiors throughout their careers. The service will provide weekly updates on its pilot program development and implementation of the JWT Operational Planning Team (OPT) that will be coordinated with Scheller, Anthony Tata, the Pentagon’s Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness, said in an Aug. 12 internal memo reviewed by The Hill. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who served in the Army National Guard, has notoriously had an issue with the military’s promotion system, blocking numerous Army, Navy and Air Force promotions to one-star general or admirals — a large quantity of them Black and female service members. The Pentagon chief has prioritized what he calls the “warrior ethos,” pushing the armed services to embrace higher physical standards and criticizing the military branches for promoting individuals based on what he has claimed, without proof, are race and gender quotas. “Real toxic leadership is endangering subordinates with low standards. Real toxic leadership is promoting people based on immutable characteristics or quotas instead of based on merit,” Hegseth told senior military leaders last year in Quantico, Va. item.title: Trump demands member nations quit 'rogue' International Criminal Court
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(AP) President Donald Trump used his address to the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday to launch a pointed attack on the International Criminal Court, calling it a “rogue institution” and urging every country that belongs to the tribunal to withdraw. “I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately,” Trump said during his speech in New York. Trump called the ICC an “evil group of people” and said the United States would not permit American service members or others to face what he described as “show trials” before an “anti-American tribunal” that he said has no jurisdiction over the United States. His remarks came as his administration is preparing its most sweeping action yet against the court. Newsmax reported Sunday, citing The Wall Street Journal, that the Trump administration is preparing sanctions against the ICC itself that could potentially cut the Hague-based institution off from much of the global financial system. Under the proposal described by the Journal, most transactions involving the ICC could be prohibited following a six- to seven-month grace period, potentially making it difficult for the court to conduct transactions in U.S. dollars. A final decision had not been made as of Sunday, but U.S. officials told the Journal the sanctions could be finalized as soon as this week, while world leaders are gathered in New York for the General Assembly, or shortly afterward. The proposed measures would mark an escalation from sanctions already imposed by the Trump administration against individual ICC officials. According to Newsmax, those previously targeted include former ICC Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan, ICC President Tomoko Akane, several judges, two deputy prosecutors and the lead prosecutor involved in the case against Israeli officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July that the administration was preparing a broader campaign against the ICC, arguing that the court's efforts to prosecute officials from countries that are not members threaten U.S. sovereignty, according to the Journal report cited by Newsmax. The United States has never ratified the Rome Statute that established the ICC and is not a member of the court. Neither is Israel. The dispute between Washington and the ICC intensified after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. The ICC said its warrants were based on alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity arising from the war in Gaza, including alleged starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution and other alleged inhumane acts. Israel has rejected the allegations and challenged the court's jurisdiction. The Trump administration has strongly backed Israel and has rejected the ICC's authority over Israeli officials. In February 2025, Trump signed an executive order imposing sanctions on the ICC, saying the court had engaged in what the White House described as “illegitimate and baseless actions” targeting the United States and Israel and specifically citing the warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant. The administration's current effort goes beyond targeting individual ICC personnel by potentially imposing restrictions directly on the institution. The ICC has also pursued cases involving Hamas leaders over the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, with prosecutors seeking warrants for senior Hamas figures accused of crimes including murder and hostage-taking. Trump's attack on the court therefore came amid both an intensifying administration campaign against the ICC and the continued dispute over its investigation into alleged crimes committed during the Gaza war. The president's comments also came during a U.N. address dominated by the broader conflicts involving Iran and Israel, as Trump warned Tehran of potentially devastating consequences if it does not reach a peace agreement with the United States. Trump's ICC remarks represented a direct challenge to the court's broader claim to international jurisdiction, with the president urging its member states to abandon the institution rather than accept its authority. © 2026 Newsmax. Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A U.S. postal worker has been charged with throwing away 300 mail-in ballots in Utah. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images file) WASHINGTON — An overwhelmed U.S. postal worker in Utah threw 300 mail-in ballots into a parking lot dumpster shortly before the state’s June 23 primary election in which both Democrats and Republicans were on the ballot, Justice Department officials said Tuesday. The 34-year-old mail carrier told investigators that he did not have a political agenda and that he tossed other mail when he ditched the ballots, Melissa Holyoak, U.S. attorney for the District of Utah, said. She said roughly 95% of voters do so by mail in the state, and it wasn’t clear yet whether they were able to eventually cast ballots. According to a government memo , Damon Matai Seei told investigators that he wanted to toss out advertisements to “lighten his workload” after feeling overwhelmed. “He claims he simply made a ‘poor decision’ out of ‘frustration’ and ‘laziness,’” the memo said. He didn’t intend to toss any ballots, they said. Seei is no longer with the U.S. Postal Service. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a charge of destruction and delay of mail. Justice Department officials held a news conference in Washington to announce the charge as part of its efforts to promote “election integrity.” Federal prosecutors have made possible voter fraud — which is rare — a priority, as President Donald Trump insists without evidence that noncitizens are voting en masse and has sought to limit mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court last week refused to allow the president’s mail-in restrictions to be enforced. Trump has repeatedly made false claims that he won the 2020 election and has falsely claimed he won the popular vote in 2016, yet the Trump administration has struggled during both terms to bring cases showing evidence of significant voter fraud . That’s despite a massive effort in Trump’s second term to obtain voter registration records from states in an attempt to determine if there were any noncitizens registered. So far during the president’s second term, the Justice Department has charged 70 voter-fraud-related cases, officials said Tuesday. More than 170 million people are registered to vote in the U.S. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said there were more cases in the works, but he didn’t provide further details or a timeline. “Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this department is committed to protecting the vote of American citizens,” he said. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, meanwhile, is revving up a long-standing election monitoring program but putting a new emphasis on “ballot security” and staffing the effort with newly hired conservative personnel who have replaced longtime career employees, hundreds of whom have departed en masse since Trump returned to office. The Civil Rights Division’s efforts to seize voter rolls have resulted in a string of court losses — with 25 courts ruling against the federal government. Voting rights experts say isolated instances of fraud do happen, as do issues with voting machines, but not on a scale that could have changed the outcome of the 2020 presidential election, which was won by Democrat Joe Biden . But the materials that the Justice Department releases could help feed Trump’s broader narrative about elections. And with the majority of voters disapproving of Trump’s presidency and saying his policies have hurt the economy , Republicans are facing a tough midterms picture. Earlier this month, the Justice Department rolled out five voting-related cases , four of which were brought against noncitizens. Last week, the Justice Department announced that 16 individuals had been charged in election-related cases, with a news release mentioning that at least 10 of them were lawful permanent residents of the United States. The defendants were originally from Mexico, Nigeria, India, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Antigua and Barbuda, Venezuela, and Colombia. There was also a defendant from Russia: Victoria Aquilina, a 42-year-old Russian national who entered the United States as an au pair in her early 20s, was charged with casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Trump — who, until he won the 2024 election, faced federal criminal charges over his efforts to overturn his 2020 loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol — said earlier this year that Republicans should “ nationalize the voting .” Democrats, meanwhile, have launched an “unprecedented” effort to combat potential disruption of the 2026 midterm elections. Seei’s next court date is Nov. 30. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment. item.title: Macron says situation in Strait of Hormuz 'was probably underestimated'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In a wide-ranging exclusive interview with ABC News' David Muir, French President Emmanuel Macron said the "main objective" of his meeting with President Donald Trump on Monday was "to find the right deal in order to open" the Strait of Hormuz and address the escalating global energy crisis that has caused the price of gas, diesel and jet fuel to spike. Macron told Muir that when the war started, "the Iranian regime discovered they had this card in their hands," in their ability to close the strait. When asked whether that was a "blind spot" for Trump, Macron responded "I will not here blame anybody. We are where we are. I think the U.S -- I mean, your country -- is the one able to fix this issue, and we need you." He added that the situation with the strait "was probably underestimated, and today we have to fix this issue." ABC News - PHOTO: French President Emmanuel Macron speaks with David Muir, anchor for ABC World News Tonight in New York City. Iran live updates: Trump says team met with Iran delegation at UN When Muir asked the French president whether he would offer up his nation's military to help reopen the strait, Macron replied, "I don't want to engage in a confrontation with any country, but we are ready to be more engaged in order to protect some capacities in order to make this transit possible, yes." Macron also criticized the decision to go to war in the first place, saying "Having a regime change by bombing a country is not something I think feasible." He added, "And for me, it's not a good option, because it doesn't work. And we did this mistake several times in the past decades." Responding to Trump's complaints that "The U.S. is spending hundreds of billions of dollars, and [European allies] are not there for us," Macron told Muir France respects the U.S. and considers itself a "good ally." Macron added "But when you want to engage people, you strategize with them, and you ask them before launching a war, and we decided not to join this war because we considered, and I still consider, it was not the right option." Russia-Ukraine: Macron says he has been able to 'convince' Trump With Macron warning about intensifying Russian threats towards Europe, Muir asked whether he believed Russian President Vladimir Putin when he said Russia has "no aggressive intentions." Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: France's Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and French President Emmanuel Macron arrive at Trump Tower in New York City, September 21, 2026, ahead of a meeting with President Donald Trump. "No," Macron responded. "I don't buy when President Putin say years ago he wanted peace and make peace. This is not true. And I don't buy when he say he doesn't -- he's not aggressive with -- with Europeans. This is not true." Macron told Muir he had a "very good discussion" with Trump regarding Russia's war in Ukraine while in New York this week. "My conviction is that your president has a fair assessment now of the situation, that Russia is not delivering what they wanted, that Ukraine is resisting with a lot of bravery and innovation, and that we have to help them," he said. Asked about his relationship with Trump, Macron told Muir that he and Trump have a "very good" relationship, and while they sometimes disagree, "we have always been extremely frank to each other." The French president said he believes Ukraine is an area where he has been able to "convince" Trump. "I think on Ukraine we worked very hard, a few of us," he said. "I hope we change his mind. And the fact that he got the conviction that Russia was overrated." Macron on Trump’s 'strange' social media map: 'Let's not create new conflicts' During the interview Tuesday, Muir asked Macron about Trump's recent social media post showing a map with the U.S. flag sprawling across North America, including French territories off the coast of Canada. Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: France's President Emmanuel Macron speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations Headquarters in New York City, September 22, 2026. "When asked about the map, you said, "People have strange ideas. They say strange things." Did you tell President Trump you thought it was strange?" Muir asked Macron. "Yes, several times," Macron responded. "Honestly, look at the situation today ... We have a war in Ukraine which is existential for the European security. We have war in the Middle East ... We have AI and all this technological race to, not to fix, but to coordinate and make sure that there is not a race to the worst between China and the U.S ... .We have sufficient topics to be fixed. Let's not create new conflicts and new tensions," Macron told Muir. And as Trump calls AI fears a " hoax ," Macron said he takes concerns that AI could pose a significant threat to humanity "very seriously." "This is why we have to make it totally clear and to have visibility, cooperation, and build new regulation on these consequences," Macron told Muir, while calling for a global discussion on the rapidly developing technology. What are the top threats posed by AI and should you be worried? "I think we should make a distinction between a pause for the frontier model and innovation and how precisely to be efficient regarding the misuses. ... It should not be just the decision of the U.S. government," he said. "It's a necessity to have a proper discussion between [the] U.S., China, Europe, and the rest of the world ... to deal with AI excesses and with AI risks for our economies and national securities." Macron on Trump's arch: 'These monuments are bigger than ourselves' Muir asked the French president about Trump's proposed " Triumphal Arch ," which Trump has said is inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. "President Trump wants to build an arch in Washington. He says it's gonna be like the one in Paris, but it'll blow it away," Muir asked Macron. Macron responded he has seen pictures of the proposed arch, and had discussed the Arc de Triomphe with President Trump "several times." Muir following up, asking "Is it gonna blow it away?" "No," Macron responded. "Paris will remain Paris and the Arc de Triomphe remain the Arc de Triomphe...These monuments are bigger than ourselves." item.title: Agency says it canceled 315,000 Obamacare health plans last month
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Bo Erickson and Christy Santhosh WASHINGTON, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is halting enrollment in Obamacare health plans for more than 760,000 enrollees it believes were fraudulently signed up, Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday, part of an ‌anti-fraud effort he estimated would save $2.2 billion in taxpayer money. The US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services canceled about 315,000 plans last ‌month, citing unverified citizenship or immigration documentation and suspected improper enrollments. The agency will bar 569 brokers it accused of submitting "statistically implausible rates of plan year 2026 applications" without necessary ​applicant information such as a Social Security number. The plans, created by Democratic President Barack Obama's signature Affordable Care Act, offer income-based subsidies. Republican President Donald Trump sought unsuccessfully in his first term to overturn the law and has proposed changes that would make the plans less comprehensive. Millions dropped coverage this year as rising medical costs and the expiration of extra COVID-era subsidies made monthly premiums unaffordable. Vance described the canceled group as "a mix of both phantom ‌people, but also real people who just don't ⁠meet the eligibility requirements," including some he said who were signed up by brokers without their knowledge. Vance said the administration would further verify between 419,000 and 450,000 more people to confirm they are legal US residents meeting ⁠income thresholds. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said the enrollees were treated as "phantoms" because officials believe most either do not exist or were unaware they had coverage, having never filed a claim and being unreachable despite repeated contact attempts. BROKER REGISTRATION FREEZE The administration is using an emergency-style rulemaking process to impose an immediate, industry-wide freeze ​on new ​Obamacare broker registrations, bypassing the usual advance notice-and-comment period. Oz called it a "temporary ​national moratorium" for six months, saying most fraud was ‌concentrated among such agents. CMS said some brokers have allegedly enrolled people without genuine consent, changed people's plans without permission, used inaccurate information, or created questionable applications to receive commissions. The agency said brokers without a 2026 registration will be frozen out until February 1, 2027. The freeze could weigh on insurers that rely on brokers to sign up customers, analysts said. ENROLLMENT IMPACT WARNING Because brokers are key to how people enroll, the freeze "may negatively affect enrollment and potentially margins related to higher risk pool in a market that is already contracting" as enhanced subsidies expire, said Morningstar analyst Julie ‌Utterback. A blanket moratorium "would punish legitimate professionals instead of targeting the bad actors responsible ​for fraud," said Mychal Walker, president of the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, ​a trade group that urged CMS to adopt targeted safeguards ​instead. CMS said unauthorized Obamacare enrollments could cost up to $6.6 billion in improper federal spending for the 2026 plan ‌year. The cancellations were led by Vance's anti-fraud task force, which ​includes Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy ​Jr., Oz and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson. CMS said it expects a return of about $2.2 billion in advance payments of the premium tax credit for the canceled enrollments. Oz said the figure would climb, calling it "the tip of the iceberg." An HHS report released ​earlier this year estimated nearly half of new ‌Obamacare enrollments between 2021 and 2024 may have been improper, phantom or fraudulent. CMS said more than 1 million enrollees ​received coverage without providing a Social Security number. (Reporting by Bo Erickson and Ahmed Aboulenein in Washington, Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; ​Additional reporting by Susan Heavey; Editing by Alexandra Hudson and Bill Berkrot) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-says-canceled-315-000-143133907.html

item.title: ICE officer who shot man in Austin was issued a bodycam but wasn't wearing it
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News. The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez , 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back. On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone. After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene. Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez was shot by an ICE officer while delivering food in Austin. (Courtesy Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch) The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said. The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements. Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed. Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.” He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said. “Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post. Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain. “We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.” Elizdar, right, wife of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, and attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. (Jay Janner / The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images) The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain. “He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said. “We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.” Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.” He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release. A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S. A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney. On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.” Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop. ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras. A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car. “I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades. “You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said. A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side. At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection. Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around. The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming. The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole. An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle. “This is unjust,” she says as she’s recording the video. Julia Ainsley reported from Washington, D.C., Daniella Silva from New York and Albinson Linares from Austin, Texas. item.title: U.S., Greenland and Denmark sign deal in bid to end Arctic standoff
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Gram Slattery and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement on Tuesday that permits a larger US military presence on Greenland and may resolve a standoff over the strategically located and mineral-rich island. The agreement, signed during Trump's visit ‌to the UN General Assembly in New York, stops short of Trump's demand that the US annex Greenland as a US territory to head off the growing ‌Arctic presence of Russia and China. But the deal does codify a greater US military presence on the icy territory, an option that emerged as Greenland leaders argued against a complete US takeover. A text of the deal released after ​the event said the US can establish a "Golden Dome" defense system in Greenland as a shield against ballistic missile threats. The shortest route from Europe to North America runs via the Arctic island, which is the location of the northernmost US military base. In his speech to the assembled world leaders at the UN before the signing ceremony, Trump said the agreement gives the US "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory." "No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval," ‌Trump said. Trump signed the agreement along with Danish Prime Minister ⁠Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen in a trilateral ceremony after Trump gave his UN speech. Frederiksen described the agreement as a deal that can "last forever" and said it underlines the importance of the NATO alliance and respects Greenland's right to self-determination. A STRONG NATO Nielsen emphasized the importance of ⁠NATO in the Arctic region. "We believe that it is vital to keep NATO strong, also in the Arctic, where the alliance has a key role to play," he said. At a press conference after the signing, Nielsen said Greenlanders must now go through a process of restoring trust with the US. Trump's threats to take the island by force had strained relations with both Greenland and Denmark. "I believe the crisis ​is ​over now, but I don't think the conflict is over in the sense that this agreement could ​very well be used - if the Americans wish - as a platform to ‌force through further concessions," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen. Greenland, a former colony and now a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, sits between the Arctic and North America and holds vast energy resources. The US already operates Pituffik Space Base in remote northwestern Greenland. The deal opens two new military sites: Narsarsuaq, a former Cold War airbase whose population has dwindled to just a few dozen, and Mestersvig, currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit. "We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate location. We will be building two very major military bases," Trump said in his UN speech. Trump's refusal to rule out military or ‌economic force to acquire Greenland triggered a diplomatic crisis in January within NATO and forced Denmark and the ​island's government into months of intensive negotiations. The text of the agreement says it amends a 1951 defense treaty ​that had been the legal basis for the US presence. It adds that Washington may ​seek further bases in the future, with details decided by mutual agreement. The deal has no end date, grants US aircraft and vessels broad access ‌across Greenland and its territorial waters, and bars non-NATO states from establishing ​military installations on the island. It also restricts foreign ​investment, effectively blocking states and investors from countries outside NATO, NATO partners and the European Union from holding control or significant influence in sectors deemed particularly sensitive, including critical infrastructure and resource extraction. The deal, which needs approval by the parliaments of Denmark and Greenland, marks a shift from Trump's earlier ambitions for an outright acquisition of ​Greenland, an island three times the size of Texas with a ‌population of only 57,000 scattered along its rugged coastline. But it represents the first major increase in US military infrastructure in Greenland since the Cold War, when the ​US maintained 17 installations and more than 10,000 personnel there. (Reporting by Gram Slattery at the UN and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen in Copenhagen; additional reporting by Stine ​Jacobsen; Writing by Steve Holland; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria, Ross Colvin, Rosalba O'Brien and Nick Zieminski) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/trump-greenland-denmark-sign-deal-163727098.html

item.title: Trump floats banning U.S. diesel exports as prices hit a record $6.52
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump said Tuesday that he would support banning exports of diesel fuel. "I've said let's not send out the diesel," the president said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. "We make a lot of diesel. It could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know, it's a sort of a flow. It's a balance." Trump added, "But no, I've called for it. I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he's examining whether a diesel export ban is feasible, given overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work. The national average price of diesel fuel has surged to an all-time record of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA , a staggering 77% increase compared to this time last year. Driven primarily by global supply crunches from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, the sudden spike is acting as a massive tax on the US supply chain, which is heavily reliant on diesel to move goods. Because diesel is the economy's primary industrial fuel, its high cost is spilling over into consumer prices nationwide. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, posted on X , "this will backfire and is not good." "U.S. diesel prices are determined not by a U.S. supply and demand balance, but a global one," De Haan wrote. "Keeping distillates and diesel [at] home does not change the world price that reference our prices. You can't fence off a globally traded commodity by executive order and expect the global price to stop applying to it." Economist Joseph Brusuelas warned that the export ban could backfire for another reason: if energy producers pull back on production. The US produces 5.3 million barrels per day, above the 3.6 million barrels of daily domestic demand. He says an export ban would create a short-term domestic surplus, which would then have to be sold at a discount. That, in turn, could cause energy firms to pull back on production, sending prices back up. Jennifer Schonberger is a veteran financial journalist covering markets, the economy, and investing. item.title: Video shows injured man on the ground in Illinois after ICE mistakenly targets U.S. citizen
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A man is recovering from injuries he sustained Sunday morning after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him in a Chicago suburb. In one video verified by NBC News, a Black man is seen sprawled on the street, near a curb, behind a black SUV in Evanston, Illinois. Two agents wearing ICE-style vests are seen standing over him. One of the agents has his face covered and is wearing a vest that reads “POLICE,” and the other appears to be pinning the man down to the ground. The man is shouting at them and can be heard saying, “I’m a f------ U.S. citizen.” According to Evanston police , the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and officers on the scene requested an ambulance. Police said they are investigating the incident, which was recorded by bystanders and gained attention after being posted on social media. One bystander in the background of the video is heard saying the ICE officers used force against the man. Other bystanders begin shouting at the man on the ground, asking him if he is OK. The ICE officers eventually get in the black SUV and drive off, leaving the man on the ground. The bystanders begin trying to help the man and call Evanston police. “I saw two agents pinning down a gentleman. They were using very rough force on him, and it looked like they really did hurt him because we had to call 911,” Miguel Angel Olivares, one of the people who witnessed the encounter, told NBC Chicago on Monday. “When we saw him, he had his jaw swollen and he had a little blood on his shirt. I’m not sure if it was the agent’s or it was his blood,” Olivares said. In a news release Sunday, Evanston police said they spoke to an ICE agent who said federal immigration officers “had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking.” After the man refused to provide identification, he was “detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention.” An Evanston police officer reported observing blood on the agent’s hands. The agent said he was injured while attempting to handcuff the individual and declined medical treatment, according to the news release from Evanston police. “Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen. He was released.” A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that their officers encountered a person who resembled someone they were targeting in an enforcement operation in Evanston on Sunday. “ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself. ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the DHS statement reads. “DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.” DHS did not state anything about the injuries the man suffered and why ICE officers did not appear to render aid. Neither the police nor DHS identified the man who was injured. Evanston police said they spoke with the injured man at a local hospital on Sunday. They “photographed and documented his injuries” as part of an ongoing investigation into the incident, police said. item.title: Bill Clinton mocks Trump's planned arch and questions Kennedy Center name fight
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Former President Clinton is knocking President Trump's plans for a triumphal arch and the efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center, saying that global challenges would be more easily dealt with if leaders "didn't care as much about who got the credit." The 42 nd president delivered opening remarks at the opening of the annual Clinton Global Initiative meeting in New York on Tuesday. As he took to the lectern, Clinton quickly referenced Trump's recent announcement that plans for a massive arch bridging Washington and Virginia would incorporate a "top grade military complex" that would be used to store drones. "I think it's important to take a few minutes to assess where we are now and the environment in which we are meeting," Clinton said. "I suppose I could take my entire allotted time to discuss the self-evident wisdom of building an Arc de Triomphe in Washington to hold all our drones," the former president said to laughs from the audience. "Some of this stuff — it's hard to make up," he added. "Over the course of a lifetime, there are only so many real opportunities to make decisions that we know will shape our personal history and the history of those we live with and care about for a long time to come. This is one of those moments," he said, before mentioning the Kennedy Center board's attempts to inscribe Trump's name on the historic Washington building. Last week, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Trump-picked board to add the president's name to the institution and to rename its campus after Trump. "I personally think that the way we've argued about what's going on at the Kennedy Center and all that kind of stuff — I think we've been majoring in the minors," Clinton said. "You really think 100 years from now anybody's going to care very much about whose name's on what building?" he asked. "Isn't it more important what happens in the building? And what happens outside the building?" he continued. "I feel so strongly — as I did 30 years ago-plus when I ran for president as a virtual child — that diversity is a positive thing, not a negative one." "That cooperation works better than conflict, and that we could actually deal with just about every challenge we face, if we didn't care as much about who got the credit, and we made sure that we took care of the least of these," Clinton, 80, said. His remarks largely focused on dealing with the development of artificial intelligence and criticizing "zero-sum thinking" by the country's political leaders. "I believe that on the 250th anniversary of this country, we can't have a politics driven by zero-sum thinking: In order for me to win, you have to lose," he said. "Nevertheless, I do understand why so many leaders around the world have chosen this zero-sum approach. Think how richly they have been rewarded for it in every sense of the word, and this payoff has been more apparent in the United States than any other country," the former commander in chief said. "Some days I can hardly believe what is happening in this country that I love so much. People in charge have created one set of rules for themselves and another set for everyone else," Clinton said, without mentioning Trump by name. "They've weaponized government to settle personal scores, prosecute enemies, stamp out free speech. They've even made the federal government a new profit center for themselves and their allies," he said. "That violates the spirit and letter of the Emoluments Clause of our Constitution."
